text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Swedish government is close to an agreement with the Centre Party on big changes to the Dennis packet regarding transportation and the road system in Stockholm. Newspaper sources say the new agreement should be made clear next week.

- The Swedish paper industry is continually trying to work out a new agreement with unions without conflict. A new eight year agreement with Arbio for 25,000 paper and pulp workers, that took effect from January 1 this year, gives a 2.6 percent wage rise over the next year. This is the first agreement settled.

- The closure of nuclear reactors at Barseback in southern Sweden will have an effect on the Swedish economy, according to the latest economic forecasts released by Nordbanken. Households' buying power will be cut by 0.5 percentage points due to higher electricity prices. Consumer prices will be 0.5 percentage points higher due to the nuclear phase out.
- Eight out of 10 Swedes are opposed to door-to-door sales or telephone sales, a new poll by the consumer organisation found.

- Insurer Trygg-Hansa posted a 30 percent higher profit of 2.4 billion crowns for 1996. The company also significantly reduced SPP's ownership through a two billion crown share buyback at a price three percent below the market price. SPP has earlier said its large holding of Trygg-Hansa was not part of its strategy. The buy-back will reduce SPP's stake to nine percent of votes and 11 percent of capital from 16 percent votes and 20 percent of capital.

- Unemployment in Sweden rose in January despite an increase in the number of jobs, figures from the Swedish Labour Board showed. The number of people unemployed rose by 33,000 people in Janaury from a year ago making 9.0 percent of the workforce unemployed. Including people on government training schemes and sponsored jobs the level of unemployment was 13.5 percent in January. The government has set a goal to halve unemployment.

- Insurer Trygg-Hansa stock rose five percent on Thursday on news that the company plans to buy back B-shares valued at two billion crowns. The redemption is primarily directed at the insurer's two largest shareholders, Tyrgg-Hansa Life and SPP. The company said the purpose of the redemption was to improve capital structure and create value for shareholders.

- Restaurant owners suffered another lean year in 1996 with turnover down by an estimated 3.3 percent compared to 1995, according to the Swedish Association of Restaurants and Hotels. This was the sector's worst year since 1993. The association said one reason is that the amount of money an employee can write-off for a business lunch has been cut to 180 crowns a person from 300 crowns.

- Roller bearing maker SKF reported a 29 percent fall in pre-tax profits to 2.4 billion crowns while turnover fell 8.5 percent to 33.6 billion crowns. Despite the fall its shares rose six crown mainly due to a positive forecast fo 1997 and a somewhat lower cut in profits than expected.

- Large amounts of stock in Ratos, a Swedish industrial holding company, was traded late on Wednesday, mainly by Ohman and Carnegie. Some of the stock was traded between the two brokers. Since Wednesday was the last day of Ratos' share redemption programme, the trading in Ratos will be reviewed by the Stockholm exchange.
